1 I find a strange knowledge of wind, an open door in the mountain pass where everything intersects. Believe me. This will not pass. This is a world where flags contain themselves, and are still, marked by their unfurled edges. Lean stuff sways on the boughs of pitch pine: silver, almost tinsel, all light gone blue and sprouting orange oils in a last bouquet. 2 These were the nest builders; I caught one last morning, I sang so it fell down, stupid, from the trees. They’re so incorrect in their dead skin. Witness their twig feet, the mistake of their hands. They will follow you. They yearn pebbles for their gullets to grind their own seed. They swallow so selflessly and die like patriots. 3 Last Christmas, a family of five woke from their dreaming and dreamed themselves over: the baby in its pink pajamas, the boy in the red flannel bathrobe he grabbed from the door, a mother, a father, and a sister in curlers; all died. A wood frame house, a cannister of oil, a match—watch as it unsettles. They were so cold; umber. 4 I am away from the knowledge of animal mystics, brujas and sorcerers or the nudging chants of a Tlingit Kachina. I am frightened by regions with wills of their own, but when my people die in the snow I wonder did the depths billow up to reach them?

# At the Confluence

I discovered it at the pass—that place where the mountains fold into each other and the wind seems to remember something ancient. There, at the convergence of ridgelines and valleys, where cold air rushing down meets warm currents rising up, I felt for the first time that I understood wind not as movement but as a language older than words. It was as if the mountain itself had chosen that narrow gap to speak through, and I, standing at the threshold where earth and sky and stone all touched, became briefly fluent in something I could not name. The knowledge came unbidden, mystical in the way that certain landscapes force revelation upon those who simply happen to stand still long enough within them.

I think of this now when I watch the birds building their nests along the cliff face below that same pass. They are not beautiful creatures, not really—their skin beneath the feathers has always struck me as somehow wrong, dead-looking, ashen in a way that seems to betray some flaw in their making. Their movements are clumsy, ungainly, all sharp angles and hesitation. And yet I have watched them swallow small stones, pebble by pebble, with a devotion that borders on the sacrificial. They do this not for themselves but for the grinding work of digestion that will let them survive, let them return to feed their young. There is something almost patriotic in this—a small, unglamorous heroism, the willingness to carry hard, indigestible things inside oneself for the sake of a larger continuance. I find myself moved by creatures I find, in truth, somewhat pitiable.

It was in winter, near Christmas, that the house at the base of the pass burned. I did not see the fire itself, only its aftermath—the blackened frame, the stillness where a family of five had lived only hours before. A baby. A boy. Their mother. Their father. A sister who might have been anywhere between the ages of the boy and the parents—I never learned exactly. All five of them gone in a single night, the warmth of their home turned suddenly, violently, against them, and then the terrible cold that followed, the cold of bodies no longer needing shelter from anything.

I do not come from people who read the wind as omen, who see in the flight of birds the movements of ancestors or gods. I was not raised among those who speak to animals as kin, who understand the pass and its convergences as thresholds between worlds. That knowledge belongs to others, to traditions I stand outside of, sometimes envying, sometimes wary. I confess I am afraid of the wild the way one is afraid of something that might have its own intentions—not malevolent, necessarily, but indifferent, vast, and unaccountable to human wanting. The natural world, when it moves with such force, seems to possess a will of its own, and I have never learned the grammar required to bargain with it or beg its mercy.

And yet, after the fire, after the family was found cold in the wreckage of what had been their Christmas, I could not stop myself from wondering—foolishly, perhaps, sacrilegiously to my own disbelief—whether the earth itself had reached upward that night. Whether something beneath the snow, some depth I have no name for and no right to invoke, had risen to take hold of them, to draw them down into itself rather than let them lie exposed and alone in the terrible open cold. I do not believe this, not in the way belief is supposed to work. But standing again at the pass, feeling the wind cross itself in that ancient confluence, I find I cannot entirely let the thought go. Perhaps it is only grief looking for a door. Perhaps grief and prayer have always been the same door, worn thin by everyone who has ever stood at a place like this and asked the wind to carry an unanswerable question back down into the earth.

# What the Mountain Knows

The wind has been talking to the pines again,
that low conversation they have every October,
secrets passed down through needles and bark
that I was never meant to understand.

I stood at the tree line yesterday
watching a hawk fall—not swoop, not dive—
fall, like something forgetting
what wings were for.
It hit the snow without sound,
and the mountain did not blink.

*Does the snow know?*

I keep asking this like a child
who has just learned that things end,
who wants the frost on the window
to explain itself, to admit
some complicity in the frozen field,
the still barn, the silence
where there used to be geese.

They tell me now, in this town
where I do not know the customs,
that a family of five burned
in their sleep last February—
mother, father, three children,
the youngest not yet two.
The house is still there, a black tooth
against the white hillside,
and no one has torn it down,
as if the emptiness itself
were a kind of shrine,
as if leaving it standing
were the only prayer they knew how to make.

I do not know what god
they kneel to here, what words
they use for grief,
whether the ash is swept
or left to scatter with the snow,
whether the depths of this lake
(I'm told it has no bottom,
though I don't believe that)
hold anything of them at all.

*Does the wind know?*

I want to ask the mountain directly—
you, who have stood here
through every fire, every winter,
every small collapse of wing and bone—
do you feel the difference
between a bird's ending
and a family's?

Or is it only weight to you,
only weather,
only the long indifferent turning
of white into white,
dark into dark,
five names becoming
snow-covered, unremarkable,
the same silence
that swallows everything eventually,
the hawk, the house,
the wind's low murmuring
that never once
has answered me.
outputs.L5:
# Believe, This, Lean

There is a quiet strength in learning to believe—not in grand, distant things, but in *this*. This moment. This breath. This imperfect, unfolding now that asks nothing of us except to be met honestly.

We often search for reasons to believe somewhere far away—in the future, in outcomes, in proof that hasn't arrived yet. But belief doesn't require certainty. It asks only for a willingness to lean forward, to lean into uncertainty rather than away from it, to lean on the people and moments that hold us up when we cannot hold ourselves.

To lean is not to fall. It is to trust that something—or someone—will meet us halfway. It is the courage to stop bracing against life and instead rest a little of our weight on what is real: this conversation, this relationship, this fragile and specific day.

Believing, then, isn't a leap into the abstract. It's a lean into the concrete. It's choosing, again and again, to say: *this* is enough to begin with. *This* is where I plant my trust. Not because everything is certain, but because leaning in—rather than standing rigid and alone—is how we discover what we're capable of carrying, and what carries us in return.

Perhaps this is the quiet work of a meaningful life: not chasing distant certainties, but believing enough in *this*—right here, right now—to lean in and see what holds.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal four-part prose poem that moves between nature imagery, a bird's death, a house fire that kills a family, and a meditation on indigenous spirituality and grief.
counterfactuals.output:
**I. The Field Before Language**

Before the field had a name, it was only breathing — grass exhaling gold into a sky that hadn't yet decided what color to be. The river ran backward some mornings, unlearning the sea. Stones held their own small weather. A doe stood at the tree line with a compass in her chest instead of a heart, and everything she looked at became north.

Here, time moved the way smoke moves — sideways, forgetful, curling back to touch what it had already left. The wind carried seeds that had not yet chosen to become anything. Even grief, in this field, was only a rumor whispered between roots, a thing waiting for a name to fall into.

**II. What the Sparrow Knew**

The sparrow fell out of the sky the way a sentence falls apart mid-thought — no drama, just a sudden absence of syntax. It had been singing about nothing in particular: a fence post, a color, the ordinary miracle of another morning. Then the singing stopped, and the small body became a punctuation mark on the frostbitten lawn.

Ants found it before the sun rose all the way. The grass did not notice. The wind kept blowing the same directionless breath it always blew, indifferent to the tiny cage of ribs collapsing into soil. And yet — some nights later — its shadow kept appearing on windowsills where no bird stood, a smudge shaped like flight, as if the world hadn't finished translating it yet.

**III. The House That Learned to Breathe Fire**

At 3 a.m. the house exhaled once, hugely, and did not inhale again. Windows opened their mouths in astonishment. The walls, which had held so many years of small kindnesses — a child's height marked in pencil, a mother's voice humming through the wallpaper — became a throat of light.

In the yard, the trees turned their leaves away, ashamed of their own coolness. Smoke rose in the shape of a family walking upstairs, the shape of a father calling a name, the shape of a name no one would say again. The fire did not hate them. Fire never hates. It only remembers being small once, being a match struck for light, before it grew enormous with hunger it did not choose.

By morning, the house was a black lung against the frost. Steam rose off the ruins like a held breath finally let go. Somewhere in the debris, a bird's nest, untouched, sat in the crook of a scorched beam — proof that something soft can survive what devours everything larger than itself.

**IV. What the Old Ones Say About Ash**

There are ways of grieving older than any single sorrow — ways that know the sparrow and the house and the field are not separate deaths but one long unfolding, the way a river doesn't end at the sea so much as become it.

The old teachings — carried in songs I was not born into, in ceremonies I can only witness from outside the fire's circle — say that the dead do not leave; they change their weather. That smoke is a language spoken between what was and what will be. That ash is not an ending but a kind of soil, patient, waiting for green.

I do not pretend to hold their grief in my mouth. I only notice how the wind, after any burning, moves the same whether it passes over a field, a bird, or a house — carrying what's left of us onward, refusing to let stillness have the final word. Somewhere, a grandmother's voice, not mine to borrow, teaches that mourning is a shape the living wear so the dead can find their way through us, gently, like light moving through smoke that has finally agreed to become sky.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate an experimental poem in numbered sections (1-4) with vivid, disorienting imagery about wind, birds, a family tragedy, and ancestral fear of nature's power.
counterfactuals.output:
# Wind-Tongue Ledger

**1.**

The wind arrives before its name does,
a fist of grandmothers pressed against the door.
Something in the eaves keeps counting—
one for the roof, one for the boy,
one for the year we stopped saying *storm*
and started saying *her*.

I was born mid-gust,
already leaning,
already practicing the shape
a body makes when it decides to stay.

**2.**

Birds fall upward here.
The starlings write and rewrite the same
black sentence across the sky,
erasing themselves into evening,
a hundred small deaths
rehearsing one large one.

My uncle used to say
crows remember the faces
that wronged them—
so when the flock split
the morning after the barn went down,
he stopped going outside bareheaded,
stopped looking up at all,
as if the sky itself
kept a ledger of our name.

**3.**

The year the river took the youngest,
no one spoke of water for a decade.
We renamed the creek *the ditch,*
called the flood *the Tuesday,*
folded the photographs backward
so the smiling stopped facing us.

Grandmother sewed a coat
from the tablecloth we ate on
that last supper together,
said *wear this when the sky turns green,*
said *the air remembers hands,*
said nothing else for years
about the boy,
the water,
the green
that comes before the tearing.

**4.**

Still, some nights the wind finds the gap
beneath the door and hums
the old warning in a key
none of us can sing back.

I go out anyway,
stand in the yard's dumb dark,
let it push against my sternum
like a hand trying to close a book
already finished.

Somewhere, an ancestor
is still running from a field,
still turning to look
at what she should not have looked at—

I am the shape her fear made
when it needed somewhere to live.
The birds keep writing.
The wind keeps counting.
I keep standing here
mistaking the terror
for an inheritance
worth keeping.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a dark, lyrical piece of prose poetry that shifts tone across four numbered stanzas—starting with mountain/wind imagery, then birds, then a tragic house fire, ending with reflections on mysticism and death in the snow.
counterfactuals.output:
# What the Wind Remembers

**I.**

The mountains keep their black teeth bared against the sky, and I have learned to love the cold the way you love a wound you keep reopening. The wind does not speak so much as it accuses—every gust a finger pointed at the valley below, at the smoke that used to rise from chimneys, at the paths now grown over with silence. I climbed here to forget my name and the mountain gave me a new one: *nobody*, *no one*, *the one who listens*. The wind has memory. It carries the screams of things that happened before language, before the first fire was struck from stone, and it does not care that I am cold, that I am small, that I am only passing through.

**II.**

The birds do not sing here—they confess. Black wings against a bruised sky, they wheel and dive like punctuation marks in a sentence God forgot to finish. I have watched the crows gather on the bare branches like mourners who arrived too early, patient in their dark suits, waiting for something to die so they might have purpose. A hawk cried once, high and thin, and it sounded like the last word of someone falling. The sparrows are gone now—eaten or frozen or simply wise enough to leave before the winter closed its fist. Only the carrion birds remain, and they know things. They know the weight of a body before it stops moving. They know exactly when to look away.

**III.**

The house burned on a night when the stars refused to hide their faces. I remember the light before I remember the sound—orange climbing the black windows like something trying to escape from inside its own skin. They say the mother went back for the child. They say this like it explains anything, like grief has grammar, like love has logic that survives the collapse of a roof. I stood in the yard and watched the family become smoke, watched their names dissolve into the shape of something that used to be a home. The fire did not apologize. Fire never does. It simply eats until there is nothing left to feed it, and then it goes looking, hungry-eyed, for the next thing it can call *warmth*.

**IV.**

They say the mystics found God in the snow because the snow does not lie—it simply covers, the way death covers, the way silence covers everything eventually. I think of the woman who walked into the white until she became part of it, until her footprints filled with more snow and there was no evidence she had ever chosen to leave. Is that not a kind of prayer? To disappear so completely that the world forgets to mourn you, because there is nothing left to point to, no shape to grieve? The old monks used to say that death is only the soul remembering it was never separate from the cold, from the wind, from the black wings circling. I lie down now where the snow is deepest. I let it fall on my open eyes. Somewhere, the mountain is still speaking, still accusing, and I have stopped needing to answer.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write something in the style of a fragmented, image-heavy poem exploring mortality, nature's indifference, and folklore—include a section about a Christmas house fire and one about shamanic traditions.
counterfactuals.output:
**What the Frost Knows**

I.
The field does not mourn.
It grows white anyway, quiet
as a mouth that has said
all its names.

Crows counting themselves
on a wire—
one for sorrow,
the rest not translated.

II. *December, a house*

The tree went up like a struck match
remembering it was once a forest.
Tinsel curling to black lace.
Someone's stocking still had a shape
for an hour, a foot of ash
holding the idea of a foot.

Outside, snow kept falling,
indifferent as a verdict,
covering the black print
the fire left in the yard
like a hand
pressed once, hard,
into wet cement.

The carolers on the corner
did not stop singing.
Why would they.
The song doesn't know
whose window it enters.

III.
Grandmother said: a bird in the house
means someone will leave it.
She never said which door.
She never said the door
could be made of flame.

IV. *The shaman speaks, or a poem pretends she does*

I drummed until my ribs
were the only weather.
I went down through the smoke-hole
of myself, past the reindeer's eye,
white and wet as a held moon.

The dead don't want much.
A little fat in the fire.
A little tobacco.
A name said correctly
so it turns like a key.

I saw my grandfather
walking backward into the birch trees,
already forgetting the walk forward
had ever happened.

The spirits don't do metaphors.
They just are the cold
you didn't dress for.

V.
Bones under snow
are just another kind of root.

The river doesn't slow down
for the shape a body made
crossing it once, badly, in spring.

VI.
What the fire taught the house:
that being loved
is not the same as being kept.

What the winter teaches everyone,
eventually, in its flat white voice—

there is no ledger.
Only weather,
and what the weather
finds standing.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a haunting, non-linear poem with four numbered parts that blend natural imagery, a cruel anecdote about birds, a devastating family death by fire, and an outsider's fear of ancestral magic.
counterfactuals.output:
**What the Smoke Would Not Say**

*i. Orchard Weather*

The apples came in late that year, small and wrong,
skins tight as drum-heads over rot.
Crows sat in the black branches counting something
none of us could name — bones, maybe, or hours.

My grandmother said the land remembers
every hand that's touched it, kindly or not,
the way a bruise remembers the thumb.
Frost came early. The well went quiet.
Something in the dirt was listening
for its name to be called wrong.

*ii. What Aunt Ruth Did With the Wrens*

She caught them for the singing, she said,
though she never let them sing.
A jar, a pin, a little thread
looped soft around the throat —
*so they'd stay*, she told us, smiling,
*so they wouldn't up and leave.*

We were children. We believed
cruelty could be a kind of love
if it was old enough, if it wore
our grandmother's hands.

I have her eyes, they tell me.
I have not yet found the jar.

*iii. The Night the Second House Burned*

Nobody agrees on how it started —
a lamp, a spark, a sleeping child's breath
too close to something that wanted out.
By morning there were four less chairs
at a table built for twelve.

We found my uncle's wedding ring
fused to a doorknob, cooling slow
like something being born backward.
The birds didn't sing for a week.
Ash sat in the well water
and none of us would drink,
though thirst, like grief, doesn't ask permission.

They say the dead stay close to fire —
that's why we salt the thresholds still,
why no one lights a candle after dark
without a word passed under breath,
a name we don't say twice.

*iv. What I Married Into*

I am the one who wasn't born here,
who flinched the first time crows
went silent as we drove up the gravel road,
who noticed how the women's hands
moved when they thought no one watched —
small circles, like winding something tight.

*Old family*, they told me, laughing,
*just old family things.*
But I have seen the jars in the cellar,
the feathers kept like rosaries,
the way this house holds its grief
the way a fist holds smoke —
open, and it all comes pouring out,
closed, and something in you starts to burn.

I married into the orchard, the crows, the ash.
I lie awake and listen
for the sound of wings
against a throat
that isn't singing.

I have not yet found the jar.
I am starting to think
it has found me.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
